an0319.user: Need a sanity check. Fintech API SaaS, running Meta for 30 days, spend ₹16.5L. Meta's dashboard says ROAS 4.5. But my Shopify shows last-click ROAS of 2.0 on the same period. That's a huge gap. Which one do I believe? What's wrong?
an0319.assistant:
Nothing is 'wrong' — you've just walked into a fight that has no winner. Meta's 4.5 is modelled conversions on a 7-day click (and post-iOS, a lot of that is statistical reconstruction). Shopify's 2.0 is last-click, which strips Meta of every assist and hands the credit to whatever touched the customer last. Both are biased, in opposite directions. The real number sits somewhere between them, and no amount of staring at the two dashboards will reconcile them — they're measuring different things and were never going to agree.

So stop refereeing. The metric that doesn't lie is blended CAC: total spend across everything ÷ actual new customers Shopify recorded that month. On ₹16.5L, if you pulled in, say, 600 genuinely new customers, that's ₹2,750 blended CAC — and you manage the account to that, not to either platform's ROAS.

Anchor on blended CAC and your contribution per customer. The two ROAS figures become directional signals — useful for 'is Meta trending up or down', useless as absolute truth.

Caveat: blended only works cleanly if Meta is your dominant paid channel right now. The day you add Google or affiliates, you'll need to hold spend on one channel steady and watch new-customer count move, or you're back to guessing.

an0320.user: I think Google's algorithm is messing with my account. Kids-coding edtech, running Performance Max. Six weeks ago my CAC was ₹301, now it's ₹553. ROAS dropped from 4.7 to 2.5. AOV is ₹1400, margins around 53%. I haven't changed anything — same creatives, same audience. Feels like Google just got greedy.
an0320.assistant:
It's not Google getting greedy — it's that you 'haven't changed anything', and that's exactly the problem. Same creatives, same audience, for six weeks. Your frequency is at 3.3, well past the ~2.5 mark where the same people have seen your ads enough times to tune them out, and your CTR is sliding right alongside it. That's the signature of creative fatigue, not an algorithm flipping a switch.

Here's why CAC doubled: when CTR falls, PMax has to buy more impressions and pricier auctions to land the same click, so your cost per acquisition climbs from ₹301 to ₹553 even though the machine is doing nothing differently. The algorithm isn't punishing you; your ads just stopped earning attention.

You're still above water — ₹1,400 × 53% − ₹553 = +₹189 per order — so there's no emergency, but that cushion is shrinking week by week and will keep shrinking until you feed the system fresh material.

The lever: new creative angles, not a budget or targeting change. And build a testing cadence — a couple of fresh concepts every two weeks — so you never again ride one winner until it dies.

One caveat: confirm the frequency number in the placement breakdown before you act. PMax buries it, and you want to be sure 3.3 is real and not an artifact of one bloated placement.

an0321.user: Okay I'm kind of freaking out. D2C nutrition brand on Meta. My CAC has gone from ₹464 six weeks ago to ₹992 now — it's basically doubled. ROAS fell from 3.4 to 1.6. AOV ₹1600, margin 54%. I didn't touch anything, same ads same audience. Is the account dying?? Do I pause everything?
an0321.assistant:
Take a breath — the account isn't dying, but it is bleeding, and I won't soften that. At ₹992 CAC your contribution is ₹1,600 × 54% − ₹992 = −₹128 per order. Every sale right now costs you money. So the urgency is real; the diagnosis just isn't the scary one you're imagining.

This is creative fatigue, plain and textbook. You said it yourself: same ads, same audience, six weeks running. Your frequency is 3.3 — past the point where your audience has seen these creatives enough times to stop noticing them — and your CTR is sliding. When clicks dry up, Meta pays more and more to find each buyer, and that's your ₹464 → ₹992 climb. Nothing broke in the algorithm. The ads just went stale.

Don't pause everything — that throws away the learnings too. Refresh the creative with genuinely new angles (new hook, new format, new pain point), and from now on rotate fresh concepts in every couple of weeks so you never ride one winner into the ground again.

Caveat: a six-week window can also catch a seasonal dip or a competitor outspending you. Refreshing creative is the right first move regardless — but if new ads don't lift CTR within two weeks, look harder at the auction around you.

an0322.user: Looking for the non-obvious read here. Vertical SaaS for clinics, Google Search. Over the last six weeks my CAC climbed from ₹670 to ₹1391 and ROAS slid from 3.0 to 1.4. AOV ₹2000, gross margin 41%. Creatives and audience are unchanged. I assume it's auction pressure / competitors bidding up my keywords. Curious what you see.
an0322.assistant:
The competitor story is the comfortable one, and it's probably not what's happening. Here's the read: your frequency is 3.4 and your CTR is sliding on the same ad copy you've run for six weeks. On Search, that combination means your ads have gone stale to the people seeing them most — your high-intent repeat searchers have learned to skip past your line. This is creative (copy) fatigue, just wearing a Search costume instead of a feed one.

Why it shows up as CAC doubling: as your CTR drops, Quality Score softens, your effective CPC rises, and Google makes you pay more for the same click. ₹670 → ₹1,391 isn't the auction getting richer; it's your ad text getting tired and the system charging you for it.

And this one's already underwater: ₹2,000 × 41% − ₹1,391 = −₹571 per order. With a 41% margin you have no cushion to absorb a CAC this high, so it needs to move now.

The lever: rewrite the ad copy with new angles — different headline promises, different RSAs, fresh sitelinks — not a bid or budget change. Then keep a rotation cadence so the copy never ossifies again.

Caveat: if competitor impression share genuinely jumped, you'd see it in the auction insights report. Check it to rule the auction story in or out — but the fatigue signature is what your own numbers are pointing at.

an0323.user: Quick one — test-prep edtech, running WhatsApp broadcast campaigns. Last 6 days I've spent ₹18K and got 24 conversions. Is my CAC good? Should I scale this or kill it?
an0323.assistant:
Honest answer: you can't know yet, and neither can I. Twenty-four conversions over six days is too small a sample to conclude anything. Any CAC you compute off it (₹18K ÷ 24 = ₹750) could swing wildly with the next ten orders in either direction — that's not a CAC, it's noise wearing a decimal point.

Scaling or killing on this is a coin flip dressed up as a decision. Let it run until you've got around 100 conversions, or a clean 2–3 week window, whichever comes first. That's the threshold where the number stops bouncing and starts meaning something.

Until then, the only useful thing to watch is direction — is daily conversion volume holding, climbing, or collapsing? Once you're near 100, send me CAC, AOV and margin and I'll tell you scale or kill for real.

an0324.user: What's wrong here? D2C footwear, blended Meta + Google. Last 30 days: 550K impressions, 10,385 clicks, CTR 1.9%, 49 orders, conversion rate 0.47%, AOV ₹1550. Targeting is broad / interest-based. The reach looks great but sales are tiny.
an0324.assistant:
Your reach looks great because it is great — and that's the trap. CTR 1.9% is perfectly healthy; people are clicking. The problem is downstream: 10,385 clicks turned into 49 orders, a 0.47% conversion rate. That's not a top-of-funnel issue, it's an intent issue.

Broad / interest-based targeting buys you exactly this — a flood of cheap, curious clicks from people browsing shoes the way they browse anything on a feed, with no plan to buy today. They click, they look, they leave. Your funnel isn't leaking at the ad; it's leaking at the gap between 'interested in footwear' and 'ready to buy footwear now'.

So stop optimising for clicks — you already win that game and it's costing you. Shift toward high-intent: on Google, exact and phrase match on buying-intent keywords with a tight negative list; on Meta, retargeting and lookalikes off actual purchasers rather than broad interests. Fewer clicks, far better conversion.

Caveat: 49 orders is a thin base, so treat 0.47% as directional, not precise. But the pattern — strong CTR, dismal CR, broad targeting — is consistent enough that I'd start tightening intent now rather than waiting for more data to tell you the same thing.

an0325.user: Bit worried about my Meta account. D2C haircare. Last 30 days I spent around 13 lakh, my average order is about ₹2050, margins are roughly 62 percent, and CAC is coming in near ₹1074. ROAS is only 1.9 which feels really low to me. CTR is about 2% and around a third of customers (32%) buy again within 90 days. Should I be cutting spend?
an0325.assistant:
Cutting would be a mistake, and the number you're scared of is the wrong one to judge by. ROAS 1.9 feels low because ROAS ignores your margin entirely. Look at what actually lands in your pocket: ₹2,050 × 62% − ₹1,074 = +₹197 per order. You're making money on every single sale, on day one, before anyone repeats.

And they do repeat — 32% within 90 days is a genuinely strong retention number for haircare. So your real LTV is well above that ₹197; the repeat orders come at near-zero acquisition cost and stack pure contribution on top.

The mechanism here is just ROAS-worship. A 62% margin means a 'low' ROAS can still be very profitable, because every rupee of revenue carries 62 paise of gross margin to cover that CAC. Founders with thin margins need a 3+ ROAS to survive; you don't.

This account shouldn't be cut — it should be scaled. Push spend up while CAC and that +₹197 contribution hold, and watch contribution per order, not ROAS, as your guardrail.

One caveat: scale in steps, not a leap. As you add budget, CAC will drift up — keep an eye on the point where ₹2,050 × 62% − CAC stops being comfortably positive. That's your real ceiling.

an0326.user: Trying to understand my Google PMax account. Home-care D2C. Over the last 8 weeks I pushed spend from about ₹7L to ₹15.3L a month. But as I scaled, my CAC went from ₹622 to ₹1038 and ROAS dropped from 1.7 all the way to 1.0. AOV ₹1050, margin 60%. I figured more budget = more sales, but it's not really working. What's going on?
an0326.assistant:
You doubled the budget and the efficiency halved — that's not a bug, it's the channel telling you it's full. You roughly doubled spend (₹7L → ₹15.3L), CAC jumped ₹622 → ₹1,038, and ROAS collapsed 1.7 → 1.0. That's the classic shape of a saturated channel.

The mechanism: PMax spent your first ₹7L on the warmest, highest-intent pockets it could find — people already searching for or primed to buy home-care. Those pockets are finite. The extra ₹8L had nowhere efficient to go, so it bought colder, more expensive reach, and your blended CAC rose to meet it. You didn't unlock more demand; you paid more to scrape the bottom of the same barrel.

At ₹1,038 CAC your contribution is ₹1,050 × 60% − ₹1,038 = −₹408 per order — the marginal spend is now actively losing money.

The lever is not more budget into the same campaign. It's new demand: fresh audiences, new creative angles, a second channel (Meta prospecting, Amazon, whatever your buyer actually uses). Pull spend back toward the level where CAC was sane, then grow by widening the top of the funnel, not by force-feeding a pool you've already drained.

Caveat: confirm this is saturation and not seasonality over an 8-week stretch — if home-care has a seasonal dip in there, some of the CAC rise is the calendar, not the ceiling.

an0327.user: I think I need to overhaul my whole YouTube strategy. D2C haircare. This week vs last week my ROAS dropped 11%. I had 105 conversions this week. Something's clearly shifting and I want to rebuild the targeting and creative before it gets worse.
an0327.assistant:
Don't touch anything. An 11% ROAS move week-over-week on 105 conversions is well inside normal variance — that's noise, not a shift. With a base that small, a handful of orders landing on Monday instead of Sunday will swing your weekly ROAS by more than 11% on its own.

Overhauling targeting and creative off one wobbly week is how founders whipsaw their accounts into the ground — you reset learnings, lose your baselines, and then react to the next random week too.

What would actually count as a signal: the same direction holding for 3–4 weeks straight, or a single move big enough to clearly clear the weekly noise (think 25–30%+, not 11%). Until you see one of those, the right action is to do nothing and let the data accumulate.

an0328.user: Dental clinic, been running YouTube ads. My CAC is ₹520 and I feel like it's too high — ROAS sits at 2.7, CTR 1.5%, AOV ₹1400. The ads team keeps blaming targeting. How do I lower my CAC?
an0328.assistant:
You're trying to fix the wrong organ. Before we touch CAC, do the contribution math: ₹1,400 × 31% − ₹520 = −₹86 per patient. You're losing ₹86 on every acquisition — and here's the killer, that's true even if your CAC were perfect. Drop CAC to ₹400 and you'd still be barely above water. The ads aren't the disease; a 31% gross margin is.

That's the mechanism everyone misses: with a margin this thin, only ₹434 of each ₹1,400 visit is even available to cover acquisition. There's almost no room. No targeting tweak, no creative refresh, no audience exclusion changes the fact that you're trying to fund a ₹520 acquisition out of a ₹434 gross-margin pool.

So the real lever isn't marketing at all — it's margin. Raise prices on the entry service, restructure your COGS, or build a higher-value bundle that lifts AOV well above ₹1,400. Get the contribution positive first; then, and only then, does optimising CAC actually pay off.

Caveat: 31% is unusually low for a clinic — double-check what's loaded into that COGS figure. If staff time or chair costs are being double-counted, your true margin may be healthier than it looks, which would change the whole picture.

an0329.user: Quick question on my Meesho Ads — D2C pet-care. CTR is only 1.6% over the last 4 weeks and I want to get it up because I think that's dragging my CAC. CAC is ₹756, ROAS 2.2, AOV ₹1650. How do I lower my CAC?

Lifting CTR won't save you, because CTR isn't what's bleeding you. Run the contribution: ₹1,650 × 30% − ₹756 = −₹261 per order. Every sale loses ₹261, and that stays true no matter how clean your click-through rate gets. The CAC question is a distraction from the real one.

The disease is the 30% gross margin. Out of a ₹1,650 order, only ₹495 is gross margin available to pay for acquisition — and your CAC is ₹756. You're spending ₹756 to unlock ₹495. The lever lives in the P&L, not the ad manager: fix COGS, raise prices, or push AOV up with bundles so each order carries more margin. Get gross margin and contribution positive first.

an0330.user: What's wrong with my account? D2C nutrition, mostly SEO/organic but tracking the economics. Numbers: AOV ₹750, gross margin 26%, CAC ₹386, ROAS 1.9, CTR 1.7%. I want to bring my CAC down — what should I change in the ads?
an0330.assistant:
Don't change anything in the ads yet — the ads aren't your problem. Here's the arithmetic that matters: ₹750 × 26% − ₹386 = −₹191 per order. You lose ₹191 on every sale, and lowering CAC alone won't dig you out — you'd have to get CAC under ₹195 just to break even, which is brutal on a ₹750 order.

The real issue is a 26% gross margin. On a ₹750 order, only ₹195 is gross margin available to spend on acquiring the customer — and you're spending ₹386. That's not a marketing inefficiency, it's a structural one. No keyword, no creative, no targeting change can make ₹386 fit inside ₹195.

The lever is margin and AOV, not ads. ₹750 is a small basket for nutrition — push it up with bundles, subscriptions, or a larger pack size, and fix the 26% COGS (supplier terms, packaging, formulation cost). Get contribution positive, then acquisition spend starts earning instead of burning.

an0331.user: My ROAS is trash and I think the Meta algorithm is broken for my account. D2C snacks brand. Last 30 days I spent ₹18L, AOV ₹1300, margin 68%, CAC ₹783, ROAS only 1.7, CTR 1.1%. 30% of buyers come back within 90 days. Should I kill the whole thing?

The algorithm's fine, and so is your account — you're reading the wrong number and scaring yourself with it. ROAS 1.7 looks like trash only because ROAS pretends your margin doesn't exist. The mechanism behind your panic is plain ROAS-worship: at a 68% margin, a 1.7 ROAS is comfortably profitable, because 68 paise of every revenue rupee is gross margin to cover CAC. Don't kill it — this is a scaling account.

an0332.user: Honestly confused. Amazon marketplace seller, running Amazon Ads. My ROAS is a healthy 3.7, AOV ₹1550, margin 46%, CAC ₹414, CTR 1.5%. Numbers look good to me but the business feels stuck — I blamed it on ad efficiency but the ads seem fine. What am I missing?
an0332.assistant:
Your ads are fine — that's exactly why you can't see the leak. ROAS 3.7 is healthy, and first-order contribution is genuinely good: ₹1,550 × 46% − ₹414 = +₹299 per order. Acquisition is working. So the problem isn't the front door; it's that there's no back room.

Look at your 90-day repeat rate: 9%. Out of every 100 customers you spend to acquire, 91 never come back. That means your entire business runs on that single +₹299 first order — your LTV barely exceeds your first-order contribution because there's almost no second order to stack on top. You're filling a bucket with no bottom, and that's why it feels stuck no matter how well the ads perform.

This is a retention problem masquerading as a growth problem. Scaling spend now just pours more customers through a one-and-done funnel at the same +₹299 ceiling — more effort, same trapped economics.

The lever: fix repeat before you touch the ad budget. Why do 91% not reorder — is it the product, the category's natural cycle, or no reason to come back? On Amazon you're partly hostage to the platform owning the customer, so lean on Subscribe & Save, insert-card offers, and pushing buyers to your own channel for round two.

Caveat: some categories are genuinely one-purchase (durable goods), and 9% would be normal there. If snacks/consumables, 9% is a crisis; if you sell something people buy once, the fix is cross-sell, not repeat.
